blogs.title: FlashAttention-3 in Plain English: How Attention Got 2x Faster on H100
blogs.description: A friendly tour of what slows Transformers down and how FlashAttention-3 speeds them up. We unpack three big ideas—using asynchrony to overlap compute and data movement, hiding softmax under matrix multiplies, and tapping FP8 with smart accuracy tricks. You will see why this hardware-aware redesign reaches up to 740 TFLOPs/s in FP16 and approaches 1.2 PFLOPs/s in FP8, and what that means for faster training and longer contexts.

blogs.title: Producer-Consumer on the GPU: The Warp Specialization Trick Behind FlashAttention-3
blogs.description: An accessible explainer of warp specialization, where some warps only move data while others only compute. We show how Hopper’s Tensor Memory Accelerator and asynchronous Tensor Cores let FlashAttention-3 run memory copies and math at the same time using a circular shared-memory buffer. You will learn how ping-pong scheduling and dynamic register allocation help keep the GPU fed and busy.

blogs.title: Hiding Softmax Latency: The Overlap That Makes FlashAttention-3 Fly
blogs.description: Softmax is slow compared to matrix multiply, but FlashAttention-3 overlaps them so the GPU’s special function units and Tensor Cores work concurrently. This post explains the two-stage pipeline that computes the next QK^T while finishing the previous PV, and performs softmax in the gaps. We keep it intuitive, touching on why this boosts utilization and what trade-offs (like register pressure) the authors balanced.

blogs.title: FP8 Without the Fear: Block Quantization and Incoherent Processing Explained
blogs.description: FP8 is fast but tricky, especially with outliers in LLM activations. We demystify FlashAttention-3’s two accuracy guards: block quantization (scaling each block independently) and incoherent processing (a lightweight random orthogonal transform that spreads out outliers). Together they cut FP8 attention error by 2.6x versus a standard per-tensor FP8 baseline, while keeping the speed gains.

blogs.title: Taming Tensor Core Layouts: Transposes and Byte Permutes for FP8 Speed
blogs.description: Why do memory layouts matter so much for FP8? This post unpacks the k-major constraint on Hopper’s FP8 Tensor Cores and how FlashAttention-3 avoids slow global-memory transposes. Learn how in-kernel shared-memory transposes (using ldmatrix/stmatrix) and small byte permutes reconcile operand and accumulator layouts so the algorithm can chain GEMMs efficiently without extra bandwidth cost.

blogs.title: Do the Numbers Back It Up? FlashAttention-3 vs FlashAttention-2, cuDNN, and Triton
blogs.description: A results-first look at the paper’s benchmarks. FlashAttention-3 delivers 1.5-2.0x speedups over FlashAttention-2 in FP16 forward (up to 740 TFLOPs/s, about 75% of H100 peak) and 1.5-1.75x in backward, and reaches close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s in FP8. For long sequences it is competitive with or faster than optimized cuDNN attention. We also recap the accuracy story: FP16 error matches FA2 and beats standard attention by keeping softmax in FP32.

blogs.title: Adopting FlashAttention-3: A Practical Guide for PyTorch and LLM Engineers
blogs.description: Everything you need to know to try FlashAttention-3 in your stack. We cover when to pick FP16 vs FP8, hardware requirements (H100-class features), and practical layout tips for FP8 (k-major expectations and in-kernel transposes). You will learn how to fuse block quantization and the random Hadamard transform with existing steps like rotary embeddings, plus notes on MQA/GQA and upcoming integrations. Code: https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention

blogs.title: Why Faster Attention Matters: Long Contexts, Multimodal Models, and What Comes Next
blogs.description: Speeding up exact attention opens doors: longer documents, high-res vision, audio and video, and huge codebases. We connect FlashAttention-3’s gains to real workloads and costs, and outline the paper’s limitations and future directions, like optimizing FP8 for small sequences and causal masks, persistent kernels, and broader support on future low-precision hardware. The takeaway: faster, accurate attention is a foundation for the next wave of AI.
